title: Arms held up (Exodus 17:8–13)
hookLine: when Moses tires, Aaron and Hur hold up his arms

cards: Try this, if you can, right where you are: lift both arms straight out and hold them there. The first few seconds are easy. Give it a minute and the shoulders start to argue.
Now stretch that to a whole afternoon, on a hilltop, in the desert sun, while below you a battle goes back and forth depending on whether your hands are up. That's Moses at a place called Rephidim.
And his arms are getting heavy.

teach.b: First, the setup. Amalek, a desert people, attacks Israel on the road. Moses tells a man named Joshua to choose fighters and go out, a name this story will hear much more of.

Moses climbs a hill with the staff of God in his hand, and two men go with him: his brother Aaron, and a man named Hur, about whom this story tells us nothing more. Second, the strange rule of the battle.
Whenever Moses holds up his hands, Israel prevails. Whenever he lets them down, Amalek prevails. The text doesn't explain why.
Third, the tiredness. Moses's hands grow heavy; he's no superhero.

teach.h: A STONE, AND A FRIEND ON EACH SIDE.
teach.b: So Aaron and Hur put a stone under him, and he sits on it. Then they stand on either side, one on the left, one on the right, and hold up his hands.
The Hebrew word for how his hands stay, steady until the sun goes down, is emunah, the word that elsewhere means faithfulness, even faith. His hands were faithful because his friends held them.

teach.h: ARMS OUTSTRETCHED: A FIGURE OF THE CROSS.
teach.b: Very early, writers like Saint Justin Martyr looked at Moses with his arms stretched wide and saw a figure of the cross: arms open, and the people saved.

Catholics still see that posture every Sunday, when the priest raises his arms to pray the great prayers of the Mass on behalf of everyone there. The story is honest that this was a battle; Exodus doesn't make war pretty.
What it holds up is something smaller and very human: even Moses couldn't do it alone.

how: At Mass, the priest prays the collect and the Eucharistic Prayer with arms raised and open, the ancient orans posture, and early Christian writers saw in Moses's outstretched arms a figure of the cross.

o: a victory shout raised after battle
the staff of God that Moses held up high

games.q: who did what at Rephidim — tap the pairs.
p: chose the fighters and went out
held up the staff on the hilltop
held up his hands, one on each side

s: Moses held his arms up alone the whole day
his hands grew heavy. Aaron and Hur sat him on a stone and held them up.
the text explains why the raised hands mattered
it only says when his hands were up, Israel prevailed. it doesn't say why.
early Christians saw Moses's outstretched arms as a figure of the cross
Saint Justin Martyr is one of the earliest to say so.

games.q: you're Aaron on the hilltop. your brother Moses can't keep his arms up any longer, and the battle below is turning. what do you do?
o: take the staff and hold it up yourself.
tell him to rest and hope for the best.
find him a stone to sit on, and hold up one of his arms.
games.why: they put a stone under him, and Aaron and Hur stand on either side holding up his hands until sunset. they don't replace him. they hold him up.

practice: Think of someone whose arms are getting heavy right now: a parent of a newborn, a friend caring for a sick spouse, a teacher at the end of the term, a priest or a nurse running on empty.
Aaron and Hur didn't fight the battle, but they brought a stone and stood on each side, so ask what your stone could be: a meal, a text, an afternoon of babysitting, a ride.
If you pray, hold that person up before God; if you don't, keep them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Emunah, steadiness, faithfulness in Hebrew: the word for how Moses's hands stayed up, held steady by two friends until sunset. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: steadiness, faithfulness. in Exodus 17:12 it describes Moses's hands, held steady till sunset.

carryVoice: Your line: hold up their arms. A stone to sit on, and a friend on each side. That's day three hundred seventy-six.
